subjective.question: Describe the structure and function of the cell membrane. (3 marks)
subjective.answer: Structure: The cell membrane (plasma membrane) is a thin, flexible and selectively permeable membrane that surrounds the cytoplasm of every cell. It is made of a double layer of phospholipids with protein molecules embedded in it (fluid mosaic model), along with some carbohydrates on the outer surface. Functions: (1) It separates the contents of the cell from the external environment and protects the cell. (2) It controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell (selective permeability). (3) It helps the cell in recognizing other cells and in receiving signals.

subjective.question: What is the cell membrane and what is the cell wall?
subjective.answer: Cell membrane: It is the thin, living, selectively permeable membrane made of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that surrounds the cytoplasm of all cells. It controls the entry and exit of substances in the cell. Cell wall: It is the rigid, non-living and fully permeable outer layer present in plant cells (also in fungi and bacteria), lying outside the cell membrane. In plants it is made mainly of cellulose. It provides shape, support and protection to the cell. Animal cells have no cell wall.

subjective.question: Label the organelles of a cell (animal cell). (5 marks) The organelles to label in a diagram of an animal cell are:
subjective.answer: 1. Cell membrane - the outer boundary of the cell. 2. Cytoplasm - the jelly-like substance in which all organelles lie; its fluid part is called cytosol. 3. Nucleus - the control centre of the cell; it contains the DNA (genetic material). 4. Nucleolus - a dense body inside the nucleus. 5. Mitochondria - the powerhouse of the cell; they produce energy (ATP). 6. Ribosomes - small granules that make proteins. 7. Endoplasmic reticulum - a network of membranes; the rough ER (with ribosomes) makes proteins and the smooth ER makes lipids. 8. Golgi apparatus (Golgi bodies) - packages and transports proteins. 9. Lysosomes - contain digestive enzymes that break down waste materials. 10. Vacuole - a small fluid-filled sac (large in plant cells). 11. Centrosome (centrioles) - present in animal cells; helps in cell division.

subjective.question: What is the importance of mitosis? (2 marks)
subjective.answer: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which one parent cell divides to produce two genetically identical daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent (diploid). Its importance is: (1) it causes growth of the body of multicellular organisms; (2) it repairs damaged tissues and replaces worn-out and dead cells; (3) it is the basis of asexual reproduction in many organisms.

subjective.question: How does a female cell create a twin baby? (How are twins produced?) Twins are produced in two ways:
subjective.answer: 1. Identical (monozygotic) twins: A single egg (female cell) is fertilized by a single sperm, and the resulting zygote splits into two separate embryos early in development. Because both babies come from the same fertilized egg, they are genetically identical and are always of the same sex. 2. Fraternal (dizygotic) twins: Two separate eggs are released and each is fertilized by a different sperm. The two babies are genetically different, like ordinary brothers and sisters, and may be of the same or different sexes.

subjective.question: Name the levels of biological organization and define each level in one line.
subjective.answer: 1. Atom - the smallest unit of an element. 2. Molecule - two or more atoms joined together. 3. Organelle - a specialized structure inside a cell that performs a specific job. 4. Cell - the basic structural and functional unit of life. 5. Tissue - a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function. 6. Organ - a structure made of different tissues that performs a specific function. 7. Organ system - a group of organs working together to perform a major body function. 8. Organism - a complete living individual. 9. Population - all individuals of the same species living in one area. 10. Community - all the populations of different species living and interacting in one area. 11. Ecosystem - a community together with its non-living environment. 12. Biosphere - the part of the Earth where all life exists.

subjective.question: What are autotrophs and heterotrophs?
subjective.answer: Autotrophs are organisms that can prepare their own food from simple inorganic substances. Green plants, algae and some bacteria are autotrophs; most of them use sunlight for this purpose (photosynthesis) and are called photoautotrophs. Heterotrophs are organisms that cannot prepare their own food and depend directly or indirectly on other organisms for food. All animals and fungi are heterotrophs; they include herbivores (plant-eaters), carnivores (flesh-eaters), omnivores, parasites and decomposers.

subjective.question: Name all the parts of the alimentary canal. (2 marks)
subjective.answer: The alimentary canal is a long tube running from the mouth to the anus. Its parts, in order, are: (1) Mouth (buccal cavity), (2) Pharynx, (3) Oesophagus (food pipe), (4) Stomach, (5) Small intestine (duodenum, jejunum and ileum), (6) Large intestine (caecum, colon and rectum), and (7) Anus. Note: The liver, pancreas and salivary glands are associated digestive glands; they are not parts of the alimentary canal itself.

subjective.question: Differentiate between arteries, veins and capillaries. (5 marks)
subjective.answer: Arteries: (1) They carry blood away from the heart to the body organs. (2) They have thick, elastic and muscular walls. (3) They have no valves. (4) Blood flows in them under high pressure. (5) They mostly carry oxygenated blood (except the pulmonary artery). Veins: (1) They carry blood from the body organs back towards the heart. (2) They have thinner and less muscular walls. (3) They have valves that prevent the backflow of blood. (4) Blood flows in them under low pressure. (5) They mostly carry deoxygenated blood (except the pulmonary vein). Capillaries: (1) They connect arteries with veins inside the tissues. (2) Their walls are only one cell thick. (3) They have no valves. (4) They are the site where exchange of oxygen, food, water and wastes takes place between the blood and the body cells.

subjective.question: Describe the formation of seeds and fruits in plants. (3 marks)
subjective.answer: In flowering plants, after pollination, fertilization takes place in the ovule inside the ovary. The fertilized egg (zygote) develops into the embryo, and the whole ovule develops into the seed; the outer covering of the ovule becomes the seed coat, which protects the embryo. At the same time, the wall of the ovary (pericarp) develops into the fruit. The fruit protects the seeds and helps in their dispersal to new places, where the seeds can germinate and grow into new plants.

subjective.question: Define the term ecology. What are the major components of ecology?
subjective.answer: Ecology is the branch of biology that studies the interactions of organisms with each other and with their physical (non-living) environment. The term was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866 (from the Greek word 'oikos', meaning home). The major components studied in ecology are: (1) Biotic components — all living things, i.e. producers (plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria and fungi); (2) Abiotic components — the non-living factors such as sunlight, temperature, water, air and soil. Ecology is studied at the levels of organism, population, community, ecosystem and biosphere.

subjective.question: What is the difference between a niche and a habitat?
subjective.answer: Habitat is the place where an organism lives — its natural home or 'address' — including the physical conditions of that place, e.g. a pond, a forest or a desert. Niche is the role or 'profession' of an organism in its ecosystem: what it eats, how it obtains its food, when it is active, and how it interacts with other organisms. In short, the habitat of an organism is its address, while its niche is its occupation or role in the ecosystem.

subjective.question: Define population diversity.
subjective.answer: Population diversity refers to the variety and variation found among the individuals of a population of a species living in an area — differences in their genetic make-up and characteristics. It is a part of biodiversity. Greater diversity within a population makes it better able to adapt to changes in the environment and to survive diseases and other stresses.

subjective.question: What is torpor? Give an example.
subjective.answer: Torpor is a short-term state of reduced body activity in animals in which the body temperature, heart rate, breathing rate and metabolic rate drop greatly, so that the animal conserves energy during unfavourable conditions such as cold weather or shortage of food. It may last for a few hours or a day, unlike hibernation, which lasts for a whole season. Example: Hummingbirds enter torpor during the night to save energy, and bats go into torpor during the day.

subjective.question: How do animals survive in hot and cold environments?
subjective.answer: In cold environments, animals survive by: (1) thick fur, feathers and a layer of fat (blubber) under the skin for insulation; (2) hibernation (long winter sleep) or torpor to save energy; (3) migration to warmer regions; (4) shivering, which produces heat in the body. In hot environments, animals survive by: (1) losing heat through sweating and panting; (2) being active at night (nocturnal habit) and resting or burrowing underground during the hot day; (3) large ears (e.g. in desert foxes) that radiate heat; (4) estivation (summer sleep) in some animals.

subjective.question: Define intrinsic growth and the biological (biotic) factors affecting it.
subjective.answer: Intrinsic rate of natural increase (biotic potential) is the maximum rate at which a population of a species can increase in size under ideal conditions, when food and space are unlimited and there are no enemies or diseases. In real life, the growth of a population is checked by biological (biotic) factors such as: availability of food, predation (being eaten by other animals), competition between organisms for food and space, diseases and parasites, and the reproductive rate of the species itself.

subjective.question: What are the major aquatic producers?
subjective.answer: The main producers in aquatic ecosystems are the phytoplankton — microscopic floating algae such as diatoms and dinoflagellates that float near the surface of the water and carry out photosynthesis. In shallow water, rooted aquatic plants and larger algae also act as producers. These producers form the base of almost all aquatic food chains.

subjective.question: Explain marine water (the marine environment).
subjective.answer: Marine water is the salt water of the seas and oceans, with an average salinity of about 3.5% (35 parts of salt per 1000 parts of water). The marine environment is the largest ecosystem on Earth, covering about 71% of the Earth's surface. It supports a great variety of life, from microscopic phytoplankton (the main producers) to the largest animals. Its main zones include the intertidal zone (between high and low tide), the pelagic zone (open water) and the deep-sea (abyssal) zone.

subjective.question: Define a biodiversity hotspot (hotspot species).
subjective.answer: A biodiversity hotspot is a region of the world that has an exceptionally large number of endemic species (species that are found nowhere else on Earth) and that is under severe threat of destruction and habitat loss. Such regions are given priority for conservation because the loss of a hotspot would mean the extinction of many unique species.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a keystone species and a foundation species.
subjective.answer: Keystone species: A species that has a very large effect on its ecosystem compared to its numbers (abundance). If a keystone species is removed, the whole ecosystem changes greatly or may collapse. Example: the sea otter, which controls sea urchins and so protects the kelp forests. Foundation species: A species that creates and defines a habitat by its physical structure and is usually abundant. It forms the base or framework of the community on which other species depend. Example: kelp and corals, and trees in a forest.

subjective.question: What are indicator species?
subjective.answer: Indicator species are species whose presence, absence, abundance or health reflects the environmental conditions and the overall health of an ecosystem. They are used to detect changes in the environment, especially pollution. For example, lichens are very sensitive to air pollution and indicate clean air, and frogs and other amphibians indicate the quality of water in ponds and wetlands.

subjective.question: What is the atmosphere and what is its role in the ecosystem?
subjective.answer: The atmosphere is the layer of gases that surrounds the Earth. It is composed mainly of nitrogen (about 78%), oxygen (about 21%), carbon dioxide, water vapours and small amounts of other gases. Its role in the ecosystem: (1) it provides oxygen for the respiration of living organisms and carbon dioxide for photosynthesis by plants; (2) its ozone layer protects life from the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun; (3) it regulates the Earth's temperature and produces weather and climate; (4) it takes part in the water, carbon and nitrogen cycles; and (5) it helps in the dispersal of seeds, pollen and spores by wind.

subjective.question: Name and describe the three zones of a river. A river is divided into three zones along its length:
subjective.answer: 1. Source zone - the uppermost part of the river, usually in hills or mountains; the water here is cold, clear, fast-flowing and rich in oxygen. 2. Transition zone - the middle part; the river becomes wider, the flow slower and the water warmer, so more species can live here. 3. Floodplain zone - the lowermost part; the water is slow-moving, muddy and rich in nutrients, and the river flows over flat floodplains before reaching its mouth.

subjective.question: How do industrial effluents destroy the environment and human life?
subjective.answer: Industrial effluents are the liquid wastes discharged by factories into rivers, canals and the ground. They contain poisonous chemicals, heavy metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium, dyes, acids and oils. They destroy the environment and human life in the following ways: (1) they pollute drinking water and make it unfit for use; (2) they kill fish and other aquatic organisms and destroy aquatic ecosystems; (3) they contaminate the soil and reduce the growth of crops; (4) poisonous substances enter the food chain and accumulate in the bodies of animals and humans (bioaccumulation); (5) they cause serious diseases in humans, such as cancers and damage to the kidneys, liver and nervous system — for example, mercury poisoning (Minamata disease).

subjective.question: Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
subjective.answer: Prokaryotic cells: (1) They have no true (membrane-bound) nucleus; their DNA lies free in the cytoplasm. (2) They have no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum. (3) They are small and simple. Example: bacteria. Eukaryotic cells: (1) They have a true nucleus enclosed in a nuclear membrane, containing the DNA. (2) They have membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus. (3) They are larger and more complex. Examples: plant and animal cells.

subjective.question: Differentiate between plant and animal cells.
subjective.answer: Plant cells: (1) They have a rigid cell wall of cellulose outside the cell membrane. (2) They contain chloroplasts, in which photosynthesis takes place. (3) They usually have one large central vacuole. (4) They have no centrosome/centrioles. Animal cells: (1) They have no cell wall; only the cell membrane is present. (2) They have no chloroplasts, so they cannot make their own food. (3) They have only small vacuoles, if any. (4) They have a centrosome with centrioles, which helps in cell division.

subjective.question: Describe the structure of the nucleus and state its functions.
subjective.answer: Structure: The nucleus is a large, spherical body surrounded by a double nuclear membrane having pores. Inside it there is a jelly-like nucleoplasm, a dense body called the nucleolus, and thread-like chromatin made of DNA and proteins, which condenses into chromosomes during cell division. Functions: (1) It contains the genetic material (DNA), which carries the hereditary information of the cell. (2) It controls all the activities of the cell, so it is called the brain or control centre of the cell. (3) It plays the main role in cell division and in passing characters to the next generation.

subjective.question: What is photosynthesis? Write its equation and state its importance.
subjective.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae and some bacteria prepare their own food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight energy trapped by the green pigment chlorophyll; oxygen is released as a by-product. Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O —(sunlight / chlorophyll)→ C6H12O6 + 6O2 Importance: (1) It produces food for almost all living organisms, directly or indirectly. (2) It releases the oxygen that animals and plants need for respiration. (3) It keeps the balance of carbon dioxide and oxygen in the atmosphere.

subjective.question: What is cellular respiration?
subjective.answer: Write its word equation. Cellular respiration is the process by which living cells break down glucose (food) in the presence of oxygen to release energy (ATP), which the cell uses for all its activities. Carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste products. Word equation: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy (ATP)

subjective.question: Define dominant and recessive alleles, with an example.
subjective.answer: Alleles are the different forms of the same gene, present at the same position on homologous chromosomes. A dominant allele is the allele that expresses itself (shows its effect) even when only one copy of it is present, i.e. in the heterozygous condition. A recessive allele is the allele whose effect is hidden in the heterozygous condition; it expresses itself only when both copies are recessive. Example: In pea plants, the allele for tallness (T) is dominant over the allele for dwarfness (t); a plant with Tt is tall, and only a plant with tt is dwarf.

subjective.question: Differentiate between haploid and diploid cells.
subjective.answer: Haploid cells contain only one set of chromosomes (n). In humans the haploid number is 23. The gametes (sperm and egg cells) are haploid, and they are produced by meiosis. Diploid cells contain two sets of chromosomes (2n) — one set from each parent. In humans the diploid number is 46. All body (somatic) cells are diploid, and they are produced by mitosis.

subjective.question: Define species, population and community.
subjective.answer: Species: A group of similar individuals that can potentially interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring. Example: all human beings belong to one species, Homo sapiens. Population: All the individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a particular time. Example: all the deer in a forest. Community: All the populations of different species living and interacting together in a particular area. Example: all the plants, animals and microorganisms in a forest together form its community.
